items.title: Jerry Hey interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 2, 2023
items.q: I went in with Quincy doing something sometime... Quincy would call me to do the arranging

ctx.x: Did anybody ever have to tell you that or did you just know it?

I guess it was a combination of listening to all of those top 40 records that I had to transcribe, and okay they’re kind of — the horns have their own thing. You know there’s a vocal and there’s the horn parts you know so it kind of got that. Then I went in with Quincy doing something sometime you know and we just kind of talked about kind of how to approach it. And he said, “Yeah, you want to stay away from the vocal and you want to try to become part of the rhythm track.” So obviously if the rhythm hits or…
Tom also said an interesting thing that you were basically the “King of the Unisons” which I thought was interesting.

items.title: Quincy Jones — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Jerry Hey has worked with me for 35 years.

ctx.x: You were one of the people who long before, when they first started having these conferences and things in the jazz area – Ken, you don’t know this – Quincy, Cannonball [Adderley] and I forget who else came out to the University of Illinois – and this was a long time before they started talking about matching up major figures with college bands. Quincy was the conductor of my band, and the soloist was Cannonball. Do you remember this?
Absolutely. You know who else was there that day? Seawind. Jerry Hey.

items.title: Jerry Hey interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 2, 2023
items.q: Well I don’t know if they, you know, really Quincy may, Foster may, but you know a lot of the other people that are more producers and less musician, you know they’re not necessarily

ctx.x: Do you ever get over the moment of, I don’t know if anxiety is the right word, but the first time you’re reading down what you arranged and you’re in the studio and the producer is there and you’re waiting to hear the comment about your parts — or do they already know sort of what it’s going to sound like?

Well I don’t know if they, you know, really Quincy may, Foster may, but you know a lot of the other people that are more producers and less musician, you know they’re not necessarily, but the reason they hired me was because they liked what I’ve done in the past, so they know, I guess they’re assuming that it’s going to be what they’re looking © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

for. You know sometimes they’ll say, “You know I’m not really sure on that one.” And okay, what can I do to make it better? But anything that I write, I don’t care, it’s their record if they don’t like it I’ll change it.
